Actual local authority and unstated exceptions are unconfirmed. The [evidence register](EVIDENCE_REGISTER.md) identifies the four selected core rules passage-rechecked and the limits on those checks.

A decision can supersede another decision **only within an identified domain, process and jurisdiction**. A job title or reporting relationship is insufficient. Specify: the issue, product/setting, professional qualification, delegated authority, current stage, patient/representative status and applicable review route.
items.field: The rule for interpreting superior decisions

items.text: The question is not simply "who is senior?" It is "whose authorized decision controls this particular issue at this stage, under which rule, subject to which review?" Cases can require several compatible permissions; one domain does not swallow all the others.
items.field: The rule for interpreting superior decisions

items.text:
| Domain | What controls it | What does not automatically override it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Patient participation/consent | Patient rights and lawful representative authority within scope | A manager, service booking or payer approval |
| Clinical recommendation/order | Authorized treating professional, license and privileges | Coder, coordinator, system administrator or call-center title |
| Professional scope/delegation | Applicable law, license, competence and permitted practice arrangement | Work assignment or higher salary/title |
| Administrative benefits | Actual plan rules and delegated administrative decision authority | Treating-clinician recommendation alone |
| Clinical coverage determination | Applicable coverage criteria and properly qualified/delegated reviewer | An intake clerk's inability to resolve the request |
| Appeal/adjudication | Properly invoked review route and qualified/independent decision-maker | Internal reporting rank outside that route |
| Policy governance | Applicable rule and designated policy-approval process | An unapproved analyst draft |
| Operational management | Actual organizational mandate, staffing and process authority | It does not itself confer prescribing, consent or appeal powers |
| Information access/privacy | Applicable purpose, rights, permissions and restrictions | Technical ability to open a record |
These are a synthesis of the cited authorities, not an invented single national organizational chart. See [authority domain graph](graphs/authority-domains.svg).

In the hospital setting, 42 CFR 482.13(b) gives patients participation and informed-decision rights, including requesting or refusing treatment. The same provision does not turn the right into an entitlement to demand medically inappropriate services. HHS representative guidance makes the extent of representative authority depend on applicable law and circumstances. Capacity, minors, emergency exceptions, guardianship conflicts and state surrogate priority are **not resolved by a generic role title**. Establish the applicable rule for the case. [A01](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-482/subpart-B/section-482.13), [A09](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/personal-representatives/index.html)

An ordering clinician's clinical instruction and a payer's coverage determination answer different questions. The payer reviewer is not made the treating doctor's supervisor. An authorization is not patient consent; it is also not a guarantee of final payment. Those boundaries are reflected in D01, D03, D10, D18 and D32. [R06](https://health.ucsd.edu/insurance-billing/paying/faq/), [A02](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-422/subpart-M/section-422.566)

| Stage | Verified scoped rule | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial anticipated partially/fully adverse medical-necessity determination | 422.566(d): physician **or another appropriate healthcare professional**, with relevant expertise, Medicare-criteria knowledge and current unrestricted professional license | A physician-only rule for every initial denial would be inaccurate; a clerk is not an appropriate substitute |
| Reconsideration of medical-necessity denial | 422.590(h): reconsiderers were not involved in the initial determination; the medical-necessity reconsidered determination is made by an appropriately expert physician | A senior initial reviewer does not become independent merely through promotion/rank |
| Remaining disputed adverse MA issues | Independent CMS-contracted entity under 422.592, with scoped forwarding requirements in 422.590 | This is the MA IRE route, not generic commercial external review |
| Implementation of reversal | 422.618 specifies effectuation by decision type and includes further-review conditions/exceptions | A favorable review and actual implementation are separate milestones |

items.text: These statements are for the specified MA route. The integrated-plan exception described in 422.566(a), decision category, other products and actual notices must be checked. The document does not silently apply the same rules to commercial insurance, Medicaid, Part D, Original Medicare or every expedited process.

items.text: CMS describes successive MA appeal levels: plan reconsideration, independent entity, adjudication, Council and district court. Eligibility, jurisdiction, filing rules and any amount-in-controversy requirements remain conditions; the ladder is not an automatic entitlement. A16 also contains an effectuation exception when the plan seeks Council review. [A11](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/appeals-grievances/managed-care-appeals-grievances/appeals-overview)

items.text: See [MA review hierarchy](graphs/ma-appeals.svg). The forward arrows mean a permitted next review, not that the later forum is the employer of the earlier reviewer.
items.field: Medicare Advantage: two different qualification rules

items.text: HealthCare.gov describes an applicable external-review process in which an insurer must accept the external outcome. The actual state/federal route, plan and eligible issue must first be identified. Do not route an MA dispute to a commercial IRO because both are called independent review. Do not assume a peer discussion is an appeal or preserves an appeal deadline. [A12](https://www.healthcare.gov/appeal-insurance-company-decision/external-review/), [R15](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/claims-payments-billing/appeals.html)
See [commercial review graph](graphs/commercial-appeals.svg). Precise deadlines and filing instructions must come from the actual process/notice; this reference is not a filing calculator.

NCSBN directs users to state Nurse Practice Acts and a scope decision framework. BLS descriptions also identify variation for NP, PA, LPN and other roles. An employer's instruction is not evidence that the person may perform a prohibited clinical task. Nursing, pharmacy, therapy and social-work professional responsibility cannot be replaced by an invented "doctor > nurse > everyone" organizational ladder. [A13](https://ncsbn.org/nursing-regulation/practice/decision-making-framework.page), [A14](https://ncsbn.org/policy/npa.page)

The [reporting examples](graphs/reporting-examples.svg) show only described relationships from UCSD R14 and Partnership R32. The latter explicitly differentiates RN, LVN, social-work and nonclinical supervisory functions. Those descriptions do not prove the hierarchy of another organization or identical professional powers for all supervisors.

For MA, 422.137 identifies UM policy-governance responsibilities; 422.101 constrains coverage criteria. Committee approval is distinct from an individual appeal. A drafter proposes policy; the designated process approves it. A system rule is not necessarily the controlling policy version. [A05](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-422/subpart-C/section-422.137), [A17](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-422/subpart-C/section-422.101)

Hospital record entries and orders have authentication requirements in 482.24. Coders, CDI, HIM and EHR personnel have different contributions; technical or documentary access does not authorize fabrication of the clinical facts. [A15](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-482/subpart-C/section-482.24)

HHS lists exceptions to the HIPAA minimum-necessary standard, including specified provider treatment disclosures/requests. That does not erase other privacy duties or make every data exchange unrestricted. Nor is it correct to require written patient authorization for every treatment exchange. Check purpose, recipient and any specially protected material. [A10](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/minimum-necessary-requirement/index.html)
Before treating this desk reference as an institution-specific operating model, record:

1. Institution, service and insurance product; governing state and professional jurisdiction.
2. Actual license, privileges, competence and applicable practice/delegation arrangement.
3. Relevant policy/version and evidence of approval/effective scope.
4. Actual organogram and assigned clinical versus administrative supervisor.
5. Patient decision-making/representation facts and appointment limits.
6. Current case stage, decision type, notice and review route.
7. Signatory/reviewer independence, expertise and conflict requirements.
8. Data-sharing purpose, permission and relevant restrictions.
9. What counts as receipt, substantive decision, implementation and completed service.
Until these facts are supplied, the exact local permission is **not established**, not "probably allowed." The profiles state useful boundaries without inventing those facts.

items.text:
| Record/diagram type | Meaning | Does not imply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEP coordination dependency | A role may need information, context or service from another role when that pathway participates | Universal predecessor, mandatory approval, employment supervision |
| F information handoff | A named artifact/message moves between roles, with suggested fields, acknowledgement and failure route | A universally mandated form or identical procedure in every institution |

Dependencies and care coordination contain feedback cycles. A global acyclic "all people must act in this order" graph would misrepresent the work. The full network is for completeness; workflow and individual-neighborhood views are for reading.

1. **Clinical origin:** C01/C03/C04/C05 documents a supported request; the function must have actual professional permission. C02/O02 can supply referral context.
2. **Administrative preparation:** O03 verifies identifiers, O04 clarifies benefits/requirements, O06 supplies authentic records, and O01 assembles/submits. These functions can overlap in one employee.
3. **Payer exchange:** O01 receives a submission receipt and responds to information requests. Clinical gaps return to the clinician; staff do not invent evidence.
4. **Outcome:** The authorized determination and applicable notice are distinct from a provider status note. O05 coordinates scheduling and remaining prerequisites; booking is not clinical clearance or completed care.
5. **Dispute:** O10/O11/P04 use the actual correction, peer-discussion or appeal route. They preserve the distinction between procedural filing and clinical argument.
Key records: F01–F06, F12–F16. Views: [provider dependencies](graphs/provider-dependencies.svg), [provider information](graphs/provider-information.svg).

1. **Intake:** U01 receives and routes the request. U02 resolves benefit/enrollment questions rather than inventing medical conclusions.
2. **Clinical review:** U03/U06/U07 applies only the permitted scope. R12/R13 provide example staged processes; D12 and D13 state the separate MA initial/reconsideration rules.
3. **Escalation:** U04 and U05 resolve the assigned clinical question. A consultation, review recommendation and authorized determination are separate work products.
4. **Notice:** U09 communicates the authorized record. U10/U11 explain or route status; their communication is not automatically a new determination.
5. **Review route:** U12 verifies the correct route/standing. In the scoped MA process, U13 and then U14 handle review as specified. U18 represents eligible commercial external review, not the MA ladder. J01–J03 are conditional later MA forums.
6. **Implementation:** A reversal is not the same event as authorization/service/payment implementation. A16 conditions remain applicable.

Key records: F07–F20, F42–F44. Views: [payer dependencies](graphs/payer-dependencies.svg), [payer/appeal information](graphs/payer-appeal-information.svg), [MA appeal hierarchy](graphs/ma-appeals.svg), [commercial review](graphs/commercial-appeals.svg).

1. **Engagement/assessment:** P01/P02/P03 supply the relevant goals, supports and authority facts; M01 identifies needs and clinical ownership. P05/P06 provide access support as needed.
2. **Plan:** M01 coordinates a shared plan while clinical, psychosocial, medication and other professionals retain their own scope.
3. **Services:** Referrals may go to social work, pharmacy, navigation, rehabilitation, nutrition, respiratory care or community supports. Availability, patient wishes and actual professional permissions determine participation.
4. **Transitions:** M18 organizes information and service arrangements. A06 governs the cited hospital setting; A07 separately identifies home-health plan/order responsibilities. Receiving acceptance must be recorded, not assumed.
5. **Follow-through:** M01/M30 tracks service status and barriers. A failed appointment or unavailable resource returns to the appropriate owner; a task label should not silently become "patient received service."
6. **Change:** Clinical changes reach the responsible clinician, resource issues reach service/management owners, and privacy/representation questions reach the appropriate channel.

Key records: F21–F36. Views: [care dependencies](graphs/care-dependencies.svg), [care information](graphs/care-information.svg). Every supporting discipline also has a separate dossier and S interface.

| Problem | Appropriate first owner | What must not be assumed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Patient/case identity mismatch | Registration/HIM, with the relevant requester | That similar names justify merging records |
| Missing clinical support | Responsible clinician or evidence author | Administrative staff can create facts |
| Wrong or unclear benefit/product | Payer benefits/designated decision owner | Clinical recommendation alone changes plan benefits |
| Reviewer lacks permission/expertise | Appropriate professional review/UM leadership | Seniority substitutes for qualification |
| Same person involved in scoped MA reconsideration | Appeal operations to assign compliant reviewer | Higher title cures initial involvement |
| Patient disagrees/refuses | Patient and responsible clinical team; lawful representative process if relevant | Coverage approval or family preference is consent |
| Caregiver/appeal representative authority unclear | Appropriate representation/privacy/legal channel | Family or a generic signature grants unlimited authority |
| Communication access failure | Qualified access service and decision participants | Silence or translated text alone proves informed understanding |
| Record access/sharing uncertain | HIM/privacy with the actual purpose and material | Either all sharing is forbidden or all is unrestricted |
| Service not available/accepted | Referring coordinator and receiving service, with clinical input | A sent referral establishes capacity |
| Clinical change during coordination | Responsible clinical professional / actual urgent pathway | A coordinator should alter treatment without authority |
| Coverage dispute | Actual peer/correction/appeal pathway | Complaint and appeal are identical |
| Favorable review not implemented | Accountable plan/process owner and applicable escalation | A favorable letter proves delivery/payment |
| Technical failure | System/access support plus clinical/process owner | IT can change clinical facts or create approval |
These ownership suggestions synthesize role duties; they are not a substitute for the institution's emergency, safeguarding, reporting or legal procedures.

For each handoff, distinguish case identity, substantive author, version/date, status and recipient. Mark whether a document is a draft, request, recommendation, determination, notice or completed-service record. The exact legally required fields differ; the F contracts label their proposed modeling fields accordingly.

Do not forward every record to every role simply because the graph shows a connection. Determine purpose and appropriate information scope; A10's treatment exception does not remove other privacy protections. The information diagrams are conceptual role/artifact maps, not a system security architecture or a list of mandatory API calls.

The diagrams describe real-world functions using public sources and explicit operational synthesis. They do not assert all 97 roles are separately simulated, prescribe an agent architecture, or derive hidden verifier requirements. Mapping to the 75 public task instructions remains a separate unperformed study.

items.text: The relevant ecosystem spans the patient, provider, insurer, delegated reviewers and community services. There is no fixed universal headcount. A role is a function, not necessarily a separate employee: referral, scheduling and authorization may be combined in one job; a physician may act as treating clinician and later join a peer discussion.

The tables cover **usual functions**, **conditional participants**, and **adjacent/oversight roles**. Those labels are qualitative synthesis, not measured prevalence. Professional authority depends on training, service, organization and applicable requirements. The map is US-focused because that is the benchmark's context.

The official benchmark names provider prior authorization, payer utilization management and care management [R01–R02]. The real-world map is broader. It does not claim every profession below is separately simulated, required for every task, or replaceable by one autonomous agent. Medication, equipment, discharge and external-review pathways are included as conditional context.

| Person | What they contribute | Participation | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patient / insured member | History, goals, preferences, decisions, barriers and changes | Central person; not necessarily contacted at every administrative step | R16, R22, R28 |
| Family member / informal caregiver / support person | Practical help, observations, appointments and plan follow-through | As needed, with appropriate involvement | R19, R24, R30 |
| Parent / guardian / healthcare proxy or other recognized personal representative | Acts within established healthcare/information authority | Conditional; authority and scope must be distinguished | R19 |
| Appointed appeal representative / advocate | Helps pursue a dispute within the appointment | Conditional; not automatically treatment-decision authority | R15–R17, R20 |
| Interpreter / translator / communication-access professional | Makes conversations or written information accessible | Conditional on communication needs | R21 |
| Patient navigator / patient-relations advocate | Helps resolve access/process obstacles or routes concerns | Conditional; training and title vary | R04, R28–R29 |

Being a caregiver does not automatically make someone a legal decision-maker. Appeal representation is a separate question. An interpreter helps communication and does not thereby become a clinician or representative [R19–R21].
This is the requesting clinic, hospital, practice or supplier arranging authorization for proposed care.

| Role | Concrete work | When involved | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ordering/treating physician | Recommends service and supplies clinical rationale and documentation | Usual clinical origin; another authorized practitioner may order | R01–R03, R11 |
| Nurse practitioner / physician assistant / other authorized practitioner | Orders or supports care within the applicable professional role | May occupy the ordering-clinician function | R11, R25–R26 |
| Referring clinician / primary-care clinician | Sends referral/history and communicates with the receiving service | When referral needed; may also be the ordering clinician | R03–R05 |
| Receiving specialist / performing clinician | Clarifies proposed service, procedure and relevant evidence | Service-specific; may also be the requester | R01–R05 |
| Clinic nurse / medical assistant / clinical-support staff | Helps collect chart information and coordinate clinician messages | Common support function; duties differ by training | R09, R24–R27 |
| Prior-authorization specialist / precertification representative | Assembles, submits and tracks requests; follows up missing information and outcomes | Central operational function | R03–R04 |
| Referral coordinator | Connects referring/receiving services and tracks referral requirements | Often combined with authorization or scheduling | R03–R05 |
| Registration / patient-access / insurance-verification staff | Checks patient identity, insurance identifiers and benefits | Usual function, not always a separate job | R03, R06 |
| Scheduler / procedure coordinator | Coordinates dates and service availability and reacts to authorization status | Linked scheduling function | R04–R05 |
| Health-information / release-of-information specialist | Processes record requests and appropriate sharing | When record retrieval/disclosure needs this function | R07 |
| Coding / clinical-documentation-integrity specialist | Resolves relevant code/documentation questions | Conditional/adjacent; not mandatory on every request | R03, R08 |
| Financial counselor / medication-assistance worker | Explains financial exposure or helps access assistance | Conditional affordability issue | R06, R09 |
| Provider denial/appeal specialist | Organizes denial reasons, paperwork and clinical support for an appeal | If a dispute occurs; some also handle later claims denials | R04, R08–R09 |
| Provider physician adviser / treating specialist in peer discussion | Discusses clinical justification with reviewing clinician | Escalation; may be an existing physician performing another task | R15 |
| Practice/patient-access supervisor | Assigns work and handles process/workload escalation | Supervisory or exceptional intervention | R03–R04, R14 |

| Participant | Contribution | Boundary | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Insurer provider-services representative / intake worker | Submission logistics, case identifiers, missing items and status | Process support is different from clinical decision authority | R12–R15 |
| Payer nurse / licensed clinical reviewer | Clinical assessment or clarification requests | May approve within program scope or route onward | R12–R13 |
| Payer physician / medical director / specialist reviewer | Escalated review and peer discussion | Coverage reviewer, not automatically the treating doctor | R12–R15, R18 |
| Outside clinician / lab / imaging / therapy evidence holder | Provides relevant reports and prior treatment records | Upstream evidence; not every technician joins the authorization exchange | R07, R22, R30 |
| Pharmacy pharmacist / specialty-pharmacy technician | Medication-specific access, paperwork or fulfillment | Conditional medication pathway | R09–R10 |
| Equipment supplier / infusion or receiving-service staff | Service-specific paperwork and fulfillment | Conditional; CMS documents practitioner/supplier involvement for equipment | R11, R30 |
| Independent external reviewer | Reviews an eligible disputed outcome | Conditional dispute route | R17 |

**Typical handoff:** clinician recommendation → provider access/authorization work → payer intake/review → provider response → scheduling or another next step. Requests can loop back for information or enter dispute paths. A benchmark task may start midway through the chain.

Mayo's example places authorization work in patient-access/finance operations [R03]. Noyes describes a specialist following requests through appeals [R04]. These explain why the everyday operator can be a dedicated coordinator while the clinician supplies the medical rationale.

This is the reviewing side of the request. A health plan can delegate functions to a medical group or other reviewer. UCSD's provider-affiliated UM example illustrates why employer and function must both be identified [R13–R14].

| Role | Concrete work | When involved | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UM intake / authorization coordinator | Receives request, creates case, collects records and routes review | Usual function | R12–R13 |
| Eligibility / benefits specialist | Checks membership/benefit information and administrative coverage questions | Often part of intake | R06, R13 |
| Nurse UM reviewer / appropriate licensed reviewer | Assesses evidence against criteria, seeks clarification and records review | Clinical review; profession varies by service/program | R12–R13 |
| Physician reviewer / medical director / physician adviser | Weighs escalated clinical issues and records appropriate determination | Pathway-dependent review and clinical oversight | R12–R15 |
| Specialty consultant / independent clinical expert | Provides expertise on specialized or complex questions | Conditional | R18 |
| Behavioral-health reviewer / designated practitioner | Reviews relevant mental-health or substance-use service requests | Conditional service | R13 |
| Managed-care pharmacist / pharmacy reviewer | Handles medication criteria, evidence and pharmacy-benefit issues | Conditional medication pathway | R10, R13 |
| Delegated-vendor / medical-group reviewer | Performs contracted intake or clinical-review functions | May fill one of the roles above | R13–R14 |
| Determination / notification coordinator | Delivers recorded outcome and relevant notices | Often part of intake/review operations | R13 |
| Member-services representative | Helps patient navigate status, explanation and contact points | As needed | R16, R32 |
| Provider-services representative | Handles operational contact with requesting practice | Common external-facing function | R15, R32 |
| Internal appeal / grievance coordinator | Receives dispute material and routes it appropriately | Conditional dispute | R15–R17 |
| Appeal clinician / specialty reviewer | Reconsiders disputed clinical issues | Process-dependent qualifications and independence | R13, R15, R17 |
| Independent external reviewer / review administrator | Reviews or administers eligible external challenge | Conditional; separate from ordinary internal review | R17 |
| SHIP counselor / consumer-assistance or ombudsman contact | Helps the patient navigate rights or the appropriate complaint/help channel | Conditional Medicare/program-specific support; not clinical reviewer | R35 |
| UM supervisor / manager | Manages queues, urgent work, quality, staffing and escalation | Supervisory; may intervene directly | R14 |
| Patient / representative / treating clinician / provider coordinator | Supplies facts, requests review, discusses case or challenges outcome | External participants, described above | R15–R17, R19–R20 |
**Typical handoff:** intake and administrative checks → clinical review → physician/specialty escalation as needed → determination and notification → appropriate reconsideration or appeal if pursued.

Martin's Point explicitly describes nonclinical information collection, licensed review and physician-adviser escalation [R12]. AZ Priority Care separately describes intake, eligibility, routing and notification work [R13]. These are concrete examples, not a universal national rule about who signs every approval or denial.

Keep benefit/administrative problems distinct from medical-necessity assessment. A peer discussion, internal appeal and independent external review are different processes. A payer UM nurse and a hospital discharge/UR nurse may have similar credentials while acting for different organizations and purposes.

Care management can be based in a clinic, hospital, insurer or community program. AHRQ-hosted guidance describes several suitable professional backgrounds depending on program needs [R23]. The title alone does not establish that a worker is an RN or can prescribe treatment.

**Typical handoff:** referral/identification → patient engagement and assessment → shared plan → work distributed to clinicians/services → follow-up and reassessment. Creating a plan and the patient actually receiving the arranged service are different milestones [R22, R25, R28].

UCLA describes clinical, social-work, advanced-practice and administrative staff working together [R25–R27]. GRACE illustrates an NP/social-worker pair supported by an interdisciplinary team [R24]. These show multiple possible team designs rather than one compulsory composition.

Do not count every executive, lawyer, technical worker or regulator as a routine participant merely because the organization employs them. Identify the function actually exercised for the case or program.

1. **Role versus person:** peer-to-peer is an interaction between existing clinicians; coordinator titles can overlap. Table rows are not a headcount.
2. **Side versus title:** identify provider, payer, delegated group and patient/community perspective. The same RN credential can underlie different responsibilities.
3. **Clinical decision versus coordination:** recommending treatment, reviewing coverage, collecting evidence, moving records and expressing patient choices carry different responsibilities.
4. **Real world versus simulation:** benchmark tasks sample this ecosystem. No claim is made that all roles are separately simulated or that one agent replaces all professions.

The closest everyday operational counterparts are a **provider authorization coordinator**, a **payer clinical-review team**, and a **care manager working with the patient and a multidisciplinary team**. This is a functional interpretation, not a formal occupational classification issued by the benchmark.

This is desk research and a source-backed synthesis, not an observed staffing census, interview study, legal scope-of-practice determination or clinical validation. Some older sources establish role examples; the ledger marks indexed-only or inaccessible material. No private handbook content was used. No agent architecture, implementation, model trial, provider API call, external message or submission was performed.
A task-by-task mapping to public agent-facing instructions remains unperformed. It could clarify which subset of these people and responsibilities appears in each specific benchmark task.

items.field: Where chi-Bench fits in healthcare work

items.text: **Evidence caution:** this explanation is an interpretation of cited public material, not a claim-by-claim factual certification. The later [evidence register](HealthcareRoles/EVIDENCE_REGISTER.md) identifies narrow passage checks and labels unconfirmed model/local-authority content.
For the extensive real-world participant map, responsibilities and handoffs, see [WORKFLOW_PEOPLE.md](WORKFLOW_PEOPLE.md) and its [source ledger](Source/04-workflow-people-sources.md).

The closest description is **healthcare operations and care coordination, with policy-grounded clinical reasoning**. The benchmark covers work performed across a healthcare provider, an insurance payer, and a care-management team. Documentation is one output; operational decisions, communication, escalation, and changes to application records are also part of the work. This classification is an interpretation of the benchmark's published task descriptions.

The official three domains are provider prior authorization, payer utilization management, and care management, with 25 core public tasks each. Agents work through simulated applications using tools. Tasks have specified starting points and completion requirements; an individual task need not cover every stage of a patient's entire journey. See the [official domain descriptions](https://github.com/actava-ai/chi-bench#what-this-benchmark-measures) and [public task explorer](https://www.actava.ai/benchmarks/tasks).

Think of a clinic or hospital trying to obtain the required insurer authorization for a proposed service. Its authorization staff may gather existing records, check coverage, assemble a request, and handle requests for more evidence. Clinicians may contribute the medical justification and participate in escalation or appeals. The benchmark's provider tasks represent parts of this work.
items.field: Provider side: arranging authorization for proposed care

items.text: For an invented example, a clinician recommends a procedure. The operational task becomes connecting the proposed procedure to the right patient's records, assembling the relevant evidence, submitting the required request, and recording or responding to its outcome. Writing a persuasive paragraph alone does not complete those steps.
items.field: Provider side: arranging authorization for proposed care

items.text: CMS describes prior authorization as a process in which the provider submits a request and receives a decision before services are rendered. That general background explains the administrative purpose; the exact benchmark workflow follows its own task and policy materials. [CMS overview](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/monitoring-programs/medicare-fee-service-compliance-programs/prior-authorization-and-pre-claim-review-initiatives).
items.field: Provider side: arranging authorization for proposed care

items.text: The second domain represents the receiving insurance organization. The benchmark describes intake, checking policy, nurse and physician review, and issuing a determination. This is utilization management: reviewing whether a requested service meets the applicable requirements and routing the case through the appropriate review stages.

There is real reasoning in this category: identifying which evidence matters, noticing that a criterion is unsupported, and identifying when another review stage is needed. But the operational question is about a request under a particular policy, rather than an unrestricted attempt to diagnose a patient from scratch. CMS's coverage material helps distinguish coverage determinations from the treating clinician's broader clinical assessment. [CMS coverage background](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coverage/determination-process).

The third domain moves closer to patient communication and care coordination. The benchmark describes chart review, contact with a simulated patient, assessments, and preparation of a care plan. Real-world analogues include nurse case managers and care coordinators; actual staffing and responsibilities vary by organization.

An invented example is a patient who has difficulty following an existing care plan. A coordinator needs to learn what is preventing follow-through, record what the patient actually says, and organize appropriate support and follow-up. The central difficulty can involve missing information, communication, and continuity across records, as well as clinical knowledge.

AHRQ describes care coordination in terms of organizing care activities and sharing information. It identifies needs assessment, proactive care planning, monitoring, follow-up, and links to community resources as examples. These explain why this domain is broader than writing hospital notes. [AHRQ care coordination](https://www.ahrq.gov/ncepcr/care/coordination.html).

| Aspect | Relationship to these tasks |
| --- | --- |
| Documentation | Necessary evidence and outputs: requests, reviews, assessments, case notes, or plans, depending on the task |
| Clinical reasoning | Interpreting existing medical evidence and using it within the assigned role and policy |
| Operational execution | Using tools, updating records, communicating, routing/escalating cases, and satisfying task completion requirements |
| Diagnosis and treatment | Clinical context can be relevant, but this is not primarily a bedside diagnostic or treatment-selection benchmark |
| Organization | Spans providers, insurers, and care-management teams; it is broader than one hospital department |

items.text: For harness research, this suggests studying case-state tracking, evidence provenance, policy retrieval, unresolved requirements, communication state, and confirmation that intended actions were actually saved. These are candidate mechanisms, not a selected architecture or demonstrated improvements. A useful controlled comparison holds the model fixed and measures the effect of harness changes with comparable task and inference budgets.
